title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 125 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 602–603 (Night 125, continuing directly from nights-124), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 125 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. Let out for one night after a year shut up with his wife, he goes to the garden and finds the lady he used to visit — “the daughter of Dalīla the trickster” — wasted with a year of waiting. When she learns he has married and has a son, her welcome turns to fury: a married man is no use to her, she says, and she calls her slave-girls, who throw him to the ground while she sharpens a knife to slaughter him. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-fifth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ عَزِيزًا قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ ثُمَّ إِنِّي دَخَلْتُ الْبُسْتَانَ وَمَشَيْتُ حَتَّى أَتَيْتُ إِلَى الْمَقْعَدِ فَوَجَدْتُ بِنْتَ الدَّلِيلَةِ الْمُحْتَالَةِ جَالِسَةً وَرَأْسُهَا عَلَى رُكْبَتَيْهَا وَيَدُهَا عَلَى خَدِّهَا وَقَدْ تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنُهَا وَغَارَتْ عَيْنَاهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna ʿazīzan qāla li-tāji al-mulūki thumma innī dakhaltu al-bustāna wa-mashaytu ḥattā ataytu ilā al-maqʿadi fa-wajadtu binta al-dalīlati al-muḥtālati jālisatan wa-raʾsuhā ʿalā rukbatayhā wa-yaduhā ʿalā khaddihā wa-qad taghayyara lawnuhā wa-ghārat ʿaynāhā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: Then I entered the garden and walked until I came to the sitting-place, and I found the daughter of the Dalīla, the trickster, sitting, and her head on her two knees and her hand on her cheek, and her colour had changed and her two eyes had sunk.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: Then I went into the garden and walked on until I came to the arbour, and there I found the daughter of Dalīla the trickster sitting with her head on her knees and her hand on her cheek; her colour had changed and her eyes were sunken.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks the story up by repeating the end of the last night. bint al-Dalīla al-muḥtāla, “the daughter of the Dalīla, the trickster”: Dalīla the trickster is the Nights’ proverbial trickster, and the article on the name suggests an epithet — “that daughter of a Dalīla” — rather than a real parentage; this is the lady of the garden whom ʿAzīz used to visit. maqʿad, “sitting-place”: a raised seat or bower in the garden.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي قَالَتِ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ عَلَى السَّلَامَةِ وَهَمَّتْ أَنْ تَقُومَ فَوَقَعَتْ مِنْ فَرْحَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾatnī qālati al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā al-salāmati wa-hammat an taqūma fa-waqaʿat min farḥatihā
sentences.l: And when she saw me she said: The praise (be) to God for the safety! And she made-to stand, and she fell from her joy.
sentences.i: When she saw me she said, “Praise be to God that you are safe!” and she tried to get up, but fell down for joy.
sentences.n: al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā al-salāma, “praise be to God for (your) safety”: the standard greeting to someone back from a journey or absence.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَحْيَيْتُ مِنْهَا وَطَأْطَأْتُ رَأْسِي ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَبَّلْتُهَا وَقُلْتُ لَهَا كَيْفَ عَرَفْتِ أَنْ أَجِئَ إِلَيْكِ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-istaḥyaytu minhā wa-ṭaʾṭaʾtu raʾsī thumma taqaddamtu ilayhā wa-qabbaltuhā wa-qultu lahā kayfa ʿarafti an ajiʾa ilayki fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: And I felt-shame before her and lowered my head; then I stepped-forward to her and kissed her and said to her: How did you know that I would come to you on this night?
sentences.i: I was ashamed before her and hung my head; then I went up to her, kissed her and said, “How did you know I would come to you tonight?”
sentences.n: ajiʾa: the print spells the subjunctive of jāʾa, “come”, اجئ, with the yāʾ serving only as the seat of the hamza (classically أجيء, ajīʾa); it is pointed here ajiʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ لَاعِلْمَ لِي بِذٰلِكَ وَاللّٰهِ إِنَّ لِي سَنَةً لَمْ أَعْرِفْ طَعْمَ النَّوْمِ وَلَمْ أَذُقْ إِلَّا أَنِّي سَهْرَانَةٌ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ فِي انْتِظَارِكَ
sentences.tr: qālat lā-ʿilma lī bi-dhālika wa-allāhi inna lī sanatan lam aʿrif ṭaʿma al-nawmi wa-lam adhuq illā annī sahrānatun kulla laylatin fī intiẓārika
sentences.l: She said: No knowledge (is) to me of that. By God, for me (it is) a year (that) I have not known the taste of sleep, and I have not tasted — except that I (am) wakeful every night in waiting-for-you.
sentences.i: She said, “I knew nothing of it. By God, for a whole year I have not known the taste of sleep, nor tasted any, but have lain awake every night waiting for you.
sentences.n: lā-ʿilma (one word in the print, لاعلم): the edition often runs lā together with the next word. inna lī sanatan lam aʿrif, “I have a year (in which) I have not known”: the colloquial way of saying how long something has gone on. lam adhuq illā annī, “I have not tasted, except that I…”: the object of “tasted” (sleep) is understood, and illā joins the sentence loosely: “nothing but this, that I was awake”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ مِنْ يَوْمِ خَرَجْتَ مِنْ عِنْدِي وَأَعْطَيْتُكَ الْبَدْلَةَ الْقُمَاشَ الْجَدِيدَةَ وَوَعَدْتَنِي أَنَّكَ تَرُوحُ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ وَتَجِيءُ
sentences.tr: wa-anā ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati min yawmi kharajta min ʿindī wa-aʿṭaytuka al-badlata al-qumāsha al-jadīdata wa-waʿadtanī annaka tarūḥu ilā al-ḥammāmi wa-tajīʾu
sentences.l: And I (have been) in that state from (the) day you went out from me, and I gave you the suit, the cloth, the new-one, and you promised me that you go to the bath and come.
sentences.i: I have been like this from the day you left me, when I gave you the new suit of clothes and you promised me you would go to the bath and come back.
sentences.n: al-badla al-qumāsh, “the suit, the cloth”: qumāsh, “fabric”, stands beside badla as a loose apposition, “the cloth suit”, a colloquial pattern. tarūḥu … wa-tajīʾu, “you go … and come”: the plain present for a promised future, as in the spoken language.

sentences.t: فَقَعَدْتُ انْتَظَرْتُكَ أَوَّلَ لَيْلَةٍ وَثَانِيَ لَيْلَةٍ وَثَالِثَ لَيْلَةٍ فَمَا أَتَيْتَ إِلَّا بَعْدَ هٰذِهِ الْمُدَّةِ وَأَنَا دَائِمًا مُنْتَظِرَةٌ لِمَجِيئِكَ وَهٰذَا شَأْنُ الْعُشَّاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaʿadtu intaẓartuka awwala laylatin wa-thāniya laylatin wa-thālitha laylatin fa-mā atayta illā baʿda hādhihi al-muddati wa-anā dāʾiman muntaẓiratun li-majīʾika wa-hādhā shaʾnu al-ʿushshāqi
sentences.l: And I sat, I waited-for-you the first night and second night and third night, and you did not come except after this span, and I (have been) always waiting for your coming — and this (is) the way of the lovers.
sentences.i: So I sat waiting for you the first night, the second and the third, and you never came until after all this time; and all this while I have been waiting for you to come, for that is the way of lovers.
sentences.n: qaʿadtu intaẓartuka, “I sat, I waited for you”: two verbs side by side with no “and”, the spoken idiom for “I sat waiting”. li-majīʾika: li-, “for”, marks the object of muntaẓira, “waiting for your coming”.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي أُرِيدُ مِنْكَ أَنَّكَ تَحْكِي لِي عَلَى سَبَبِ غِيَابِكَ عَنِّي هٰذِهِ السَّنَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-innī urīdu minka annaka taḥkī lī ʿalā sababi ghiyābika ʿannī hādhihi al-sanata
sentences.l: For I want from you that you tell to me about the cause of your absence from me this year.
sentences.i: Now I want you to tell me why you have stayed away from me this whole year.”
sentences.n: urīdu minka annaka taḥkī, “I want from you that you tell”: colloquial for Classical urīdu an taḥkiya; and ḥakā ʿalā, “tell about”, where Classical has ḥakā ʿan.

sentences.t: فَحَكَيْتُ لَهَا فَلَمَّا عَلِمَتْ أَنِّي تَزَوَّجْتُ اصْفَرَّ لَوْنُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ḥakaytu lahā fa-lammā ʿalimat annī tazawwajtu iṣfarra lawnuhā
sentences.l: And I told (it) to her, and when she knew that I had married, her colour went-yellow.
sentences.i: So I told her, and when she learned that I had married, she turned pale.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لَهَا إِنِّي أَتَيْتُكِ هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ وَأَرُوحُ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma qultu lahā innī ataytuki hādhihi al-laylata wa-arūḥu qabla ṭulūʿi al-nahāri
sentences.l: Then I said to her: I have come to you this night, and I go before the rising of the day.
sentences.i: Then I told her, “I have come to you tonight, but I must go before daybreak.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ أَمَا كَفَاهَا أَنَّهَا عَمِلَتْ عَلَيْكَ الْحِيلَةَ وَتَزَوَّجَتْ بِكَ وَحَبَسَتْكَ عِنْدَهَا سَنَةً كَامِلَةً حَتَّى حَلَّفَتْكَ بِالطَّلَاقِ أَنَّكَ تَعُودُ إِلَيْهَا مِنْ لَيْلَتِكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat a-mā kafāhā annahā ʿamilat ʿalayka al-ḥīlata wa-tazawwajat bika wa-ḥabasatka ʿindahā sanatan kāmilatan ḥattā ḥallafatka bi-al-ṭalāqi annaka taʿūdu ilayhā min laylatika qabla ṭulūʿi al-nahāri
sentences.l: And she said: Did it not suffice her that she worked on you the trick and married you and shut-you-up with her a year complete, until she made-you-swear by the divorce that you return to her from your night before the rising of the day?
sentences.i: And she said, “Was it not enough for her to play her trick on you, marry you and keep you shut up with her a whole year, and then even make you swear on pain of divorce to go back to her that same night before daybreak?
sentences.n: ḥallafatka bi-al-ṭalāq, “she made you swear by divorce”: an oath on pain of divorce, so that breaking it would end the marriage of itself. tazawwajat bika, “she married you”: bi- marks the person married, as in the spoken language.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَسْمَحْ نَفْسُهَا لَكَ بِأَنْ تَتَفَسَّحَ عِنْدَ أُمِّكَ أَوْ عِنْدِي وَلَمْ يَهُنْ عَلَيْهَا أَنْ تَبِيتَ عِنْدَ أَحَدٍ مِنَّا لَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً بَعِيدًا عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam tasmaḥ nafsuhā laka bi-an tatafassaḥa ʿinda ummika aw ʿindī wa-lam yahun ʿalayhā an tabīta ʿinda aḥadin minnā laylatan wāḥidatan baʿīdan ʿanhā
sentences.l: And her soul did not grant to you that you take-your-ease with your mother or with me, and it was not easy upon her that you pass-the-night with one of us one night, far from her.
sentences.i: She could not bring herself to let you go out for your pleasure to your mother’s house or to me, nor could she bear that you should spend a single night with either of us, away from her.
sentences.n: samaḥat nafsuhu bi-, “his soul allowed (something)”: bi- marks what is granted, here “that you take your ease”. tafassaḥa, “take one’s ease, go out for pleasure”: a post-classical sense, common in Egyptian Arabic. lam yahun ʿalayhā, “it was not easy upon her”: she could not bear it.

sentences.t: فَكَيْفَ حَالُ مَنْ غِبْتَ عَنْهَا سَنَةً كَامِلَةً وَأَنَا عَرَفْتُكَ قَبْلَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-kayfa ḥālu man ghibta ʿanhā sanatan kāmilatan wa-anā ʿaraftuka qablahā
sentences.l: So how (is) the state of one (whom) you were-absent from her a year complete — and I knew you before her?
sentences.i: Then what of the woman you stayed away from for a whole year — and I knew you before she did?
sentences.n: The print itself puts a fatḥa on the tāʾ of غبتَ, “you were absent”, to show it is “you” and not “I”.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ رَحِمَ اللّٰهُ بِنْتَ عَمِّكَ عَزِيزَةَ فَإِنَّهَا جَرَى لَهَا مَالَمْ يَجْرِ لِأَحَدٍ وَصَبَرَتْ عَلَى مَالَمْ يَصْبِرْ عَلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ وَمَاتَتْ مَقْهُورَةً مِنْكَ وَهِيَ الَّتِي حَمَتْكَ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: wa-lākin raḥima allāhu binta ʿammika ʿazīzata fa-innahā jarā lahā mā-lam yajri li-aḥadin wa-ṣabarat ʿalā mā-lam yaṣbir ʿalayhi aḥadun wa-mātat maqhūratan minka wa-hiya allatī ḥamatka minnī
sentences.l: But God have mercy on the daughter of your uncle, ʿAzīza! For there befell her what did not befall anyone, and she was-patient over what no one was patient over, and she died crushed by you; and she (was) the one who protected you from me.
sentences.i: But God have mercy on your cousin ʿAzīza! What happened to her has happened to no one else, and she bore what no one else could bear, and she died broken-hearted because of you — and it was she who protected you from me.
sentences.n: mā-lam (مالم, one word in the print, twice): mā, “what”, run together with lam. maqhūra, “overpowered, crushed”: in this text the word for dying of grief and wrong suffered.

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ أَظُنُّكَ تُحِبُّنِي فَخَلَّيْتُ سَبِيلَكَ مَعَ أَنِّي كُنْتُ أَقْدِرُ مَا أُخَلِّيكَ تَرُوحُ سَالِمًا بِشَحْمٍ وَأَقْدِرُ عَلَى حَبْسِكَ وَهَلَاكِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu aẓunnuka tuḥibbunī fa-khallaytu sabīlaka maʿa annī kuntu aqdiru mā ukhallīka tarūḥu sāliman bi-shaḥmin wa-aqdiru ʿalā ḥabsika wa-halākika
sentences.l: And I used to think you love me, so I let-go your way, although I was able (that) I not let-you go safe with fat, and (was) able for your imprisoning and your destroying.
sentences.i: I thought you loved me, so I let you go your way, though I could have kept you from getting off safe and sound, and could have shut you up and destroyed you.”
sentences.n: aqdiru mā ukhallīka, “I am able (that) I do not let you”: mā is the spoken negative, and aqdiru is followed directly by the verb with no an. sāliman bi-shaḥm, literally “safe with fat”: apparently an idiom for getting away unharmed, “with your fat still on you”; it is not in the classical dictionaries, so the sense is our best reading. aqdiru ʿalā, “able to”: ʿalā marks what one has the power to do.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَتْ بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَاغْتَاظَتْ وَاقْشَعَرَّتْ فِي وَجْهِي وَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيَّ بِعَيْنِ الْغَضَبِ
sentences.tr: thumma bakat bukāʾan shadīdan wa-ightāẓat wa-iqshaʿarrat fī wajhī wa-naẓarat ilayya bi-ʿayni al-ghaḍabi
sentences.l: Then she wept a weeping intense, and grew-enraged, and bristled in my face, and looked at me with the eye of anger.
sentences.i: Then she wept bitterly and flew into a rage; she bristled at me and looked at me with angry eyes.
sentences.n: iqshaʿarra, “shudder, bristle (of the skin)”: here of rage turned on ʿAzīz, “she bristled in my face”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهَا عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ ارْتَعَدَتْ فَرَائِصِي وَخِفْتُ مِنْهَا وَصَارَتْ هِيَ مِثْلَ الْغُولَةِ الْمَهُولَةِ وَصِرْتُ أَنَا مِثْلَ الْفُولَةِ عَلَى النَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhā ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati irtaʿadat farāʾiṣī wa-khiftu minhā wa-ṣārat hiya mithla al-ghūlati al-mahūlati wa-ṣirtu anā mithla al-fūlati ʿalā al-nāri
sentences.l: And when I saw her in that state, my shoulder-muscles trembled and I feared her, and she became like the ghoul-woman, the dreadful, and I became like the bean on the fire.
sentences.i: When I saw her like that I trembled in every limb and was afraid of her; she had become like a dreadful ogress, and I like a bean on the fire.
sentences.n: irtaʿadat farāʾiṣī, “my farīṣas trembled”: the farīṣa is the flesh between shoulder and breast that quivers in fear, a fixed phrase for terror. al-ghūla al-mahūla … al-fūla ʿalā al-nār: a jingle — ghūla, “ogress”, rhymes with mahūla, “dreadful”, and with fūla, a single bean jumping in the pan.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِي مَابَقِيَ فِيكَ فَائِدَةٌ بَعْدَ مَا تَزَوَّجْتَ وَصَارَ لَكَ وَلَدٌ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lī mā-baqiya fīka fāʾidatun baʿda mā tazawwajta wa-ṣāra laka waladun
sentences.l: Then she said to me: There remained not in you (any) use, after you married and there came-to-be for you a child.
sentences.i: Then she said to me, “There is no use left in you, now that you have married and have a child.
sentences.n: mā-baqiya (one word in the print): mā, “not”, run together with the verb. baʿda mā, “after (that)”: the conjunction “after”, followed by a past verb.

sentences.t: فَأَنْتَ لَا تَصْلُحُ لِعِشْرَتِي لِأَنَّهُ لَا يَنْفَعُنِي إِلَّا الْعَزَبُ وَأَمَّا الرَّجُلُ الْمُتَزَوِّجُ فَإِنَّهُ مَا يَنْفَعُنَا بِشَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-anta lā taṣluḥu li-ʿishratī li-annahu lā yanfaʿunī illā al-ʿazabu wa-ammā al-rajulu al-mutazawwiju fa-innahu mā yanfaʿunā bi-shayʾin
sentences.l: So you are not fit for my company, because none profits me except the bachelor; and as for the man, the married-one, he does not profit us in anything.
sentences.i: You are no longer fit to be my companion, for only an unmarried man is any good to me; a married man is no use to us at all.
sentences.n: The print has المتزوح, a misprint for المتزوج, al-mutazawwij, “married”, corrected here. ʿishra, “companionship, intimate company”; li- marks what one is fit for.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ بِعْتَنِي بِالْحُزْمَةِ الدَّفِرَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad biʿtanī bi-al-ḥuzmati al-dafirati
sentences.l: And you have sold me for the bundle, the stinking-one.
sentences.i: You have sold me for that stinking bundle.
sentences.n: bi- marks the price: “sold me for”. al-ḥuzma, “the bundle (of sticks or herbs)”, and al-dafira, “stinking” (Lane: dafir, of a foul smell): an insult for the wife, but the image is not otherwise known, so the exact force is uncertain.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ لَابُدَّ لَأُحَسِّرَنَّ تِلْكَ الْعَاهِرَةَ عَلَيْكَ وَلَا تَبْقَى لِي وَلَا لَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-allāhi lā-budda la-uḥassiranna tilka al-ʿāhirata ʿalayka wa-lā tabqā lī wa-lā lahā
sentences.l: By God, no escape — I shall surely make that whore grieve over you, and you will remain neither for me nor for her!”
sentences.i: By God, I will make that whore grieve for you, and you shall belong neither to me nor to her!”
sentences.n: lā-budda (one word in the print): “there is no escape”, i.e. “certainly”, here followed directly by the oath-form la-uḥassiranna, “I will surely cause grief”. ḥassara ʿalā, “make (someone) grieve over (something lost)”: ʿalā marks the loss. The “whore” is ʿAzīz’s wife.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا صَرَخَتْ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً فَمَا أَشْعُرُ إِلَّا وَعَشَرَةُ جَوَارٍ أَتَيْنَ وَرَمَيْنَنِي عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā ṣarakhat ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan fa-mā ashʿuru illā wa-ʿasharatu jawārin atayna wa-ramaynanī ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: Then she cried a cry great, and I do not perceive except that ten slave-girls came and threw me on the ground.
sentences.i: Then she let out a great shriek, and before I knew it ten slave-girls had come and thrown me to the ground.
sentences.n: fa-mā ashʿuru illā wa-, “and I do not perceive except (that)”: the set phrase for something that happens before one knows it, told in the present.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا بَقِيتُ تَحْتَ أَيْدِيهِنَّ قَامَتْ هِيَ وَأَخَذَتْ سِكِّينًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā baqītu taḥta aydīhinna qāmat hiya wa-akhadhat sikkīnan
sentences.l: And when I remained under their hands, she rose, she, and took a knife,
sentences.i: When I was pinned beneath their hands, she got up and took a knife,
sentences.n: baqītu, “I remained”: in this text baqiya often means simply “become, end up”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَأَذْبَحَنَّكَ ذَبْحَ التُّيُوسِ وَيَكُونُ هٰذَا أَقَلَّ مِنْ جَزَائِكَ عَلَى مَا فَعَلْتَ مَعِي وَمَعَ ابْنَةِ عَمِّكَ قَبْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat la-adhbaḥannaka dhabḥa al-tuyūsi wa-yakūnu hādhā aqalla min jazāʾika ʿalā mā faʿalta maʿī wa-maʿa ibnati ʿammika qablī
sentences.l: and said: I shall surely slaughter you the slaughter of the he-goats, and this will be less than your requital for what you did with me and with the daughter of your uncle before me.
sentences.i: and said, “I will slaughter you as he-goats are slaughtered, and even that will be less than you deserve for what you have done to me, and to your cousin before me.”
sentences.n: dhabḥa al-tuyūs, “the slaughter of he-goats”: the verbal noun as an accusative of manner, “as goats are slaughtered”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرْتُ إِلَى رُوحِي وَأَنَا تَحْتَ يَدِ جَوَارِيهَا وَتَعَفَّرَ خَدِّي بِالتُّرَابِ وَرَأَيْتُهَا تَسُنُّ السِّكِّينَ تَحَقَّقْتُ الْمَوْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓartu ilā rūḥī wa-anā taḥta yadi jawārīhā wa-taʿaffara khaddī bi-al-turābi wa-raʾaytuhā tasunnu al-sikkīna taḥaqqaqtu al-mawta
sentences.l: And when I looked at my soul, and I under the hand of her slave-girls, and my cheek was-befouled with the dust, and I saw her whetting the knife, I made-certain-of the death.
sentences.i: When I looked at myself, held down by her slave-girls with my cheek rubbed in the dust, and saw her sharpening the knife, I was sure that I was going to die.
sentences.n: naẓartu ilā rūḥī, “I looked at my soul”: rūḥ in the spoken sense “self”, “I looked at myself, my plight”. bi-al-turāb: bi-, “with”, the dust that grimed his cheek.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
